headline: ChatGPT now reads bank statements for Plus users, GPT-5.6 restricted by White House, Japan funds AI anime subs
summary: ChatGPT's personal finance feature is now available to all Plus subscribers, connecting to 12,000+ financial institutions via Plaid. OpenAI's new GPT-5.6 models (Sol, Terra, Luna) faced White House restrictions due to cyber capabilities.
details: ChatGPT's personal finance feature, previously Pro-only, is now accessible to all $20/month Plus subscribers. Users can connect over 12,000 financial institutions via Plaid to analyze transactions and get plain-language answers to financial queries.

Connecting a bank account to any AI involves a significant security decision, not just a convenience upgrade. Users are advised to carefully review privacy settings before linking their financial data.

OpenAI shipped three new models: Sol, Terra, and Luna, but the White House requested restricted access. Sol reportedly matches Mythos 5 in cyber capability, which is the US government's benchmark for flagging models.

This situation echoes previous instances, such as Anthropic's Fable 5 being blocked in June. OpenAI itself has stated that they don't believe such restrictions should become the long-term default. Pricing for Luna ($1/M tokens) and Sol ($5/M tokens) is public, with general availability expected within weeks.

Japan's METI is investing $70 million (¥11.5B) to cover 50% of AI translation and localization costs for anime subtitles. This initiative aims to close the gap between official translations (weeks/months) and fan subs (same day), which cost the industry an estimated ¥5.7 trillion in piracy losses in 2025.

Partners in this effort include Crunchyroll, Shueisha, Bandai Namco, Kodansha, and Square Enix. The goal is to expand the official global subscriber base from 100 million to 300 million, following a strategy successfully modeled on South Korea's KOCCA program.
These developments highlight a pattern where AI tools are rapidly moving from research labs into critical sectors like personal finance, government security, and global entertainment simultaneously.

headline_marked: [[iMessage 2FA fixes SMS pumping fraud]] costing companies millions
headline: iMessage 2FA fixes SMS pumping fraud costing companies millions
summary: SMS pumping schemes drain 2FA budgets by tricking companies into paying for fake verification messages. A new mobile-originated iMessage 2FA approach reverses the flow, eliminating the fraud incentive and high costs.
details: SMS pumping, also known as Artificially Inflated Traffic (AIT), is a scam where bad actors abuse SMS one-time code forms. They input thousands of premium phone numbers they control, causing companies to send (and pay for) messages that generate revenue for the fraudsters. Elon Musk claimed Twitter lost ~$60M/year to this before restricting SMS 2FA.

The core issue is that companies pay for outbound application-to-person (A2P) SMS messages, creating a direct financial incentive for scammers to trigger as many as possible. This makes SMS 2FA an unpredictable, exploitable, and expensive infrastructure component.

The solution lies in flipping the direction to mobile-originated (MO) 2FA, where the user sends a message to the company to prove device possession. This eliminates outbound codes, per-message payouts, and the monetization opportunity for bot farms.

Modern MO verification, especially over iMessage, offers significant advantages. Users send a one-time code from their own Apple ID via end-to-end encrypted iMessage, making it spoof-resistant and phishing-resistant.

This approach requires no outbound SMS, no per-code billing, and no A2P registration, simplifying the authentication flow. Blooio offers an iMessage API for developers to integrate this secure and cost-effective 2FA method.
